strengths: Well-motivated problem articulating fundamental tension between sample and computational efficiency in program learning
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures, training regimes, hyperparameters, and 11+ algorithmic tasks
Learned programs are interpretable by construction with insightful reasoning traces demonstrating LLM's problem-solving process
Robust empirical results showing SGD systematically fails across extensive ablations, suggesting fundamental limitation rather than tuning artifact
Technically sound formalization of SGD lower bounds through reduction to statistical query framework (Proposition 2)
weaknesses: No theoretical analysis of the proposed LLM-ERM method itself—lacks sample complexity guarantees, convergence analysis, or characterization of task solvability; claim of 'recovering statistical efficiency' lacks formal support

Unfair experimental comparison: LLM-ERM uses pretrained model trained on massive web corpus while SGD baselines train from scratch on 200 examples; this conflates inductive bias benefits with algorithmic improvements
Limited theoretical novelty: Proposition 2 primarily reformulates established SQ lower bounds from Feldman et al. (2018); Proposition 1 is standard PAC learning
No computational cost analysis despite significant practical relevance—LLM calls have 20-minute timeouts and substantial latency; wall-clock time comparison missing entirely
Scope restricted to synthetic, clean-labeled algorithmic tasks with symbolic structure favoring LLMs; no guidance on applicability to real-world problems
Critical experimental details unexplored: sensitivity to k attempts, distribution of distinct programs generated, LLM model size ablations, prompt design sensitivity
Reproducibility concerns: results depend entirely on proprietary GPT-5; experiments not reproducible without this specific model
Overclaiming: 'remarkable length generalization' only occurs for dimension-invariant rules; interpretability benefits oversold as all code is not universally interpretable

strengths: Well-motivated problem articulating genuine tension between statistical and computational efficiency in program learning
Sound theoretical analysis with clear PAC bounds and rigorous SQ hardness results (Prop 3.1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 13 algorithmic tasks with multiple strong baselines including tool-augmented LLMs and agentic systems
Impressive empirical results showing perfect/near-perfect accuracy with m=200 examples while SGD fails with 100k examples; demonstrates length generalization beyond training sequences
Clean separation of concerns: LLM provides proposal distribution while validation performs ERM-style selection; maintains interpretability with executable programs and auditable reasoning traces
Honest limitations discussion and proper ablations (prompts, hyperparameters, data scaling); transparent reproducibility details
weaknesses: Limited scope restricted to synthetic algorithmic tasks; no improvement on realistic tabular datasets (Table 4) where method is only competitive, not superior
Critical dependence on specific LLM: massive performance variance across models (e.g., FP ranges from 50% to 100%; Table 1) raises questions about attribution
Theory-practice gap: Prop. 4.1 assumes discrete enumeration but practice uses continuous sampling; key quantity p_ε(S_tr) never empirically measured or validated
Failure on pseudorandom functions (SHA ~50% accuracy) not adequately explained; unclear characterization of when method should work vs. fail
Computational cost significant at training (2.091 sec/sample vs 0.345 for FT) but not prominently discussed; limits practical adoption
SQ hardness result (Prop 3.1) requires universality over all k-parities; generality beyond planted k-parity family understated
Reproducibility limited without access to frontier LLMs; open-weight variants substantially weaker, and method requires expensive API calls
Missing empirical analysis of proposal mass and Prop. 4.1 sensitivity; no investigation of how proposal quality affects generalization
